global-economics-33bf8e58f8.headline: India’s record foreign deposit push could cost RBI $10.6 billion: Why the diaspora fundraising drive may p
global-economics-33bf8e58f8.fulltext:
India’s record-breaking diaspora fundraising drive may prove costly for the country’s central bank, leaving it with a potential $10.6 billion price tag, according to economists.
The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) special deposit program drew far more money than expected, with inflows set to rise further once overseas foreign currency debt and external commercial borrowings are included, economists say.
“Market focus has now shifted to the consequences of these inflows for RBI’s liquidity stance and operations,” said A. Prasanna, an economist with ICICI Securities Primary Dealership, referring to the haul as ‘a problem of plenty.’
The inflows, through the special window that was offered in June to shield the rupee from sliding after hitting record lows, come at a cost for the RBI.
Under the foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR(B), program, the central bank agreed to shield banks from losses if the rupee weakens, through a favourable currency-swap facility estimated to cost 3-3.5% a year. It will also need to absorb some of the extra cash pumped into the banking system as banks exchange the dollars they raised for rupees.
The two operations could cost as much as Rs.1.2 lakh crore ($12.7 billion) over five years, according to an analysis by Madhavi Arora, economist with Emkay Global Financial Services.
The RBI did not immediately reply to an email sent seeking details on the cost.
For now, the RBI doesn’t see the cost as a major concern because the final bill will depend partly on how the dollar proceeds are invested, according to a person familiar with the RBI’s thinking.
Repayment is unlikely to pose a major problem as India’s foreign-exchange reserves are expected to rise over the years from about $730 billion now and provide enough buffer to cover the amount raised. The person asked not to be identified because the matter isn’t public.
One risk is the potential impact on the RBI’s dividend to the government. The central bank transferred a record 2.87 trillion rupees in May, compared with 2.69 trillion rupees a year earlier.
Any reduction in the dividend could make it harder for the government to meet its budget targets.
“The funds raised, therefore, need to be deployed judiciously and productively to mitigate these first-order and second order fiscal costs,” Emkay Global’s Arora said.
The RBI could offset some of those costs by investing the dollars abroad. If the money is invested in 10-year US Treasuries yielding about 4.7%, the RBI could earn more in interest than it spends on hedging.
“On a net basis, per year cost could be as low as 100 billion rupees, or even marginally positive for the RBI,” said Gaura Sengupta, economist at IDFC First Bank.

For now, the RBI doesn’t see the cost as a major concern because the final bill will depend partly on how the dollar proceeds are invested, according to a person familiar with the RBI’s thinking.
Repayment is unlikely to pose a major problem as India’s foreign-exchange reserves are expected to rise over the years from about $730 billion now and provide enough buffer to cover the amount raised. The person asked not to be identified because the matter isn’t public.
One risk is the potential impact on the RBI’s dividend to the government. The central bank transferred a record 2.87 trillion rupees in May, compared with 2.69 trillion rupees a year earlier.
Any reduction in the dividend could make it harder for the government to meet its budget targets.
“The funds raised, therefore, need to be deployed judiciously and productively to mitigate these first-order and second order fiscal costs,” Emkay Global’s Arora said.
The RBI could offset some of those costs by investing the dollars abroad. If the money is invested in 10-year US Treasuries yielding about 4.7%, the RBI could earn more in interest than it spends on hedging.
“On a net basis, per year cost could be as low as 100 billion rupees, or even marginally positive for the RBI,” said Gaura Sengupta, economist at IDFC First Bank.

LIC gets RBI nod to raise ICICI Bank stake to 9.99%; ₹59.39 trillion AUM gives insurer room to deepen exposure
ADVERTISEMENT
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has approved Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) to acquire an aggregate holding of up to 9.99% in ICICI Bank, potentially more than doubling the state-owned insurer’s existing stake in the private lender.
ICICI Bank disclosed the approval in a stock exchange filing, saying it received a copy of the RBI’s letter, dated September 4, 2026, at 9:09 pm on the same day.
The approval allows LIC to acquire up to 9.99% of the bank’s paid-up share capital or voting rights within one year. If the acquisition is not completed within that period, the RBI approval will stand cancelled. The clearance is also subject to applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.
LIC already holds 4.35% in ICICI Bank
LIC held 31.18 crore ICICI Bank shares, equivalent to 4.35% of the bank’s net paid-up capital, at the end of June 2026. The RBI approval therefore provides the insurer with headroom to increase its holding by another 5.64 percentage points, taking its total stake to 9.99% if it utilises the entire approval.
Importantly, the regulatory clearance does not mean LIC has already purchased the additional shares. It gives the insurer permission to make the acquisition within the stipulated one-year window.
The development also underlines LIC’s growing presence in India’s banking sector. As of June 2026, insurance companies collectively held 8.24% of ICICI Bank, with LIC accounting for more than half of that holding. SBI Life Insurance held another 1.43%. Mutual funds, meanwhile, collectively owned 29.60% of the private lender.
LIC’s ₹59.39 trillion AUM gives it significant investment firepower
The ICICI Bank approval comes as LIC continues to deploy its enormous investment portfolio across Indian equities. Its assets under management stood at ₹59.39 trillion at the end of Q1 FY27, while investment income rose 6% year-on-year to ₹1.09 trillion during the quarter.
LIC’s latest regulatory disclosures for June 2026 also list ICICI Bank among its major equity investments, underscoring the lender’s importance within the insurer’s portfolio.
The RBI’s decision follows a similar regulatory clearance that allows LIC to raise its holding in other large private-sector banks. For ICICI Bank, however, the approval potentially gives the country’s largest institutional investor substantially greater exposure to one of India’s biggest private lenders.

world-7a2141c214.headline: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
world-7a2141c214.fulltext:
US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”
He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.
He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

Germany is planning a broad package of measures to strengthen its defences against drone attacks, cyber intrusions and other forms of Russian sabotage after a failed airport drone attack last month, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Sunday.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper, which first reported the plans, that Russia’s hybrid attacks had become a part of daily reality.
“These attacks will increase, but we can defend and protect ourselves,” Dobrindt was quoted as saying.
Russia has long rejected allegations it is carrying out operations in western Europe and has denied involvement in the German airport attack, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying the accusations were “the start of a real war”, according to state news agency TASS.

other-interests-f32c7e4fb0.headline: It felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquiet | John Harris
other-interests-f32c7e4fb0.fulltext:
“If you want me to pay my taxes,” sang the 23-year-old man on the stage, loudly accompanied by the thousands in front of him, “You better come over with a crucifix/ You’re gonna have to nail me down.”
Last Thursday night, I stood in a field in Dorset, and watched the headlining attraction on the first night of the End of the Road festival. Geese are a rock group from New York, led by the extremely talented Cameron Winter, who has a lot to say, and an often gnomic, veiled way of saying it. But the meaning of the most celebrated lines on his band’s most recent album – Getting Killed – might be clearer than a lot of the rest.
There are hundreds of different interpretations online of a song simply called Taxes, from death and martyrdom to the avoidance of responsibility. He may just, I suppose, be telling the Internal Revenue Service to go away in the cause of small-state libertarianism. But at the risk of ridicule, I’ll opt for the most literal and crowd-pleasing reading: that Winter is inspirationally updating the idea of rock music sneering at the powers that be and rejecting whatever it is they want. When I first heard those lines, in fact, I imagined him being cornered by Donald Trump, JD Vance and some or other Maga goon squad, wearily exhaling and sending them on their way.
For at least a decade now, rock – which is to say, stuff largely made with guitars and mostly delivered by bands – has been in an increasing state of cultural eclipse. Its presence in what remains of the singles chart is usually minimal-to-nonexistent; it tends to fare better in the albums rankings, but chronically lacks its old ability to push itself to the forefront of its era.
It’s striking, then, that Geese’s somewhat belated rise has been powered by an album that consummately embodies its time, has received praise to match and is evidently loved by younger people who were supposed to have long ago become largely rock-phobic (for proof, see the footage of Geese’s performance at this year’s Reading festival). Their current high profile has been powered not just by Getting Killed, but Winter’s much more intimate solo album – titled Heavy Metal – and a one-man performance at Carnegie Hall in New York, about to be released as a film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson. Seemingly as a matter of contractual obligation, all four members of his group (including guitarist Emily Green) have hairstyles like those of the early-1970s Rolling Stones, but the music they now make – their first album came out in 2018 – usually suggests something immeasurably more contemporary.
It is variously tender, soothing, angry and explosive, prone to tumble into lengthy improvisation, and sometimes shot through with knowingness that can be maddening, but is presumably the result of working in an artistic field now full of cliches that either have to be acknowledged or swerved around. But when they play live, power, ferocity and sudden snaps between loudness and calm take precedence. Some moments are redolent of Led Zeppelin, but taken somewhere completely different by the lyrical content. Radiohead are another oft-cited reference point, which feels more satisfactory, but only in the sense that Geese largely stay true to the idea that they should sound like no one but themselves and damn the consequences.
This is an age in which a huge amount of popular music is tailor-made for audiences assumed to be in a constant state of distraction, so songs often have the briskest of intros and the crassest, most earworm-ish hook lines. Geese’s music, by contrast, is often gnarly and difficult, and entails friction between the musicians and their listeners. It took me six or seven plays to even start to get my head around Getting Killed, but in an occasionally masochistic way, I enjoyed every minute.
And this, I think, is why. From its title onwards, Getting Killed is full of flickers and flashes of the volatile and frightening condition of both Geese’s home country and the wider world. Among the first words on the album, repeated five times, are “There’s a bomb in my car”, quickly followed by “My daughter is dead.” Other lyrics seem – seem – to reference the crazed ringmaster who has led the US into both internal conflict and disastrous entanglements abroad: “All people/In times of war/Must go down to the circus,” Winter sings on a piece titled 100 Horses, following that up with “There is only dance music in times of war/But we have danced for too long.” What you really yearn for is a zinger akin to Bob Dylan’s “even the president of the United States/Sometimes must have to stand naked.” But Winter’s facility with words suggests he will soon get there, even if he is currently too keen on bathetically bursting his own lyrical bubble and thereby avoiding the “spokesperson for a generation” deadweight that Dylan found so irksome: “There were hundred horses dancing/Maybe 124,” he sings at one point, which isn’t even that funny.
But such slip-ups are rare. At the core of what Geese do is something that is also sharply generational. It’s surely one of the identifying features of people their age that even comparative material comfort (all four were privately educated) doesn’t make the anxiety that comes with being the canaries in the coalmine of digital capitalism unavoidable. The title track puts this point plainly: “I’m getting killed by a pretty good life,” wails Winter. “Getting killed by a pretty good life/I have been fucking destroyed by the city tonight.” A track titled Half Real suggests twentysomethings so understandably confounded that they just want to switch off. On Thursday, Winter sang with such ferocity that any lingering suspicions about archness or humour instantly vanished: “I’ve got half a mind/To just pay for the lobotomy/And tell ’em get rid of the bad times/And get rid of the good times too/I’ve got no more thinking to do.”
On the face of it, there may be reasons to keep your distance: their comparatively privileged backgrounds, or a spurt of controversy about the ubiquity and craftiness of their (very common) online marketing. But their empathetic kind of excellence makes those things almost irrelevant. What they excel at is reflecting their audience’s experiences, feelings, passions and furies back at them. At End of the Road, evidence of that connection was consistently there on the giant screen next to the stage. The younger members of the audience pressed against the barrier at the front rejoiced in every note of Taxes, and sang along most loudly to that eternal rebuke to the hypocrisies of power and influence: “Doctor, heal yourself.” But what was most telling was the ecstatic exchange between the band and their core crowd triggered by a simple line from one of Winter’s love songs, which seemed to take on quite another meaning: “I see myself in you.”
They would doubtless hate me for saying so, but still: right now, Geese sound like the accidental representatives of a global demographic that may look sensitive and gentle, but that – in response to the impossibility of just about everything – may yet explode. In that sense, the simplest of messages is woven into what they do: look out.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

other-interests-e45b8d8551.headline: Prince’s Timeless opens another door into his extraordinary musical vault
other-interests-e45b8d8551.fulltext:
Prince’s Timeless opens another door into his extraordinary musical vault
Picture: Getty Images
Prince’s vault has never been short of mythology. What makes Timeless intriguing, then, is not merely the promise of unheard music, but the chance to hear an artiste who spent nearly four decades refusing to compromise. Across 10 recordings stretching from 1977 to 2016, the collection catches Prince at wildly different points in his evolution.
That is also the album’s central contradiction. Timeless is fascinating as an excavation but uneven as an album. Sequenced chronologically, it moves from the teenage exuberance of I Am You through the punk-funk charge of the original Tick, Tick, Bang, the atmospheric Heaven and gospel-tinged I Wonder, before reaching the lush With This Tear, later recorded by Celine Dion.
The early stretch is where the collection makes its strongest case. I Am You already contains the sensuality, falsetto and genre-fluid instincts that would become central to Prince’s identity. Tick, Tick, Bang is especially revealing: rawer and more jagged than the version eventually heard on Graffiti Bridge, it sounds less like a finished song than a glimpse of an idea Prince would keep turning over until he found another shape for it.
Then comes With This Tear, the collection’s emotional centre. Hearing Prince’s own performance of a song he wrote for another artiste gives it an intimacy that makes the track feel less like a discarded demo.
The later material is more erratic but often more revealing. Calabama finds Prince turning his frustrations with the music business into funky, horn-driven satire, while The Guilty Ones lets a sharp guitar attack cut through. Bestest Friend, meanwhile, offers a glimpse of his later-period funk sensibility.
Yet the chronological sequencing works better as an archive than as an album. Prince understood the album as a world in itself, with songs interacting, contrasting and creating momentum. Timeless instead feels governed by the dates on the tape boxes. The final live How Come U Don’t Call Me Anymore? is a beautiful reminder of his stage presence, but its placement feels more like the closing of a historical record.
And perhaps that is the fairest way to hear Timeless. It is not the lost Prince masterpiece some vault releases might tempt us to imagine. Nor does it need to be. Its value lies in the fragments: the unfinished thought, the alternate arrangement, the song that could have gone somewhere else.
For 41 minutes, Timeless offers something arguably more valuable than perfection — evidence of the restless mind behind it. Prince’s greatness was never simply that he made extraordinary records. It was that he kept making, experimenting and moving.

other-interests-aee9c66e19.headline: One of the world's darkest paints makes everything look like a black hole – and it could save our night sky
other-interests-aee9c66e19.fulltext:
A new study of one of the world’s darkest coatings suggests it could dramatically reduce the impact of satellites on astronomy.
Researchers at the University of Surrey found that the ultra-black coating Vantablack 310 could make satellites faint enough to approach the brightness limits recommended by the International Astronomical Union for protecting astronomical observations.
In Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the team report that Vantablack 310 reflects only around two per cent of incoming light and reduces bright flashes by scattering light more diffusely.
Read more
They measured the coating’s reflectivity under a range of illumination and viewing conditions to simulate how satellites painted with it would appear from the ground.
Their simulations suggest the painted satellites could have their apparent brightness significantly reduced to around magnitude +7.0, making them effectively too faint to be seen by most naked-eye observers.
This comes as concern grows over the impact of satellite megaconstellations.
Tens of thousands more are expected to be operating in low Earth orbit by the end of the decade, creating bright streaks and flares that interfere with observations and large-scale surveys of the night sky.
Lead author Astha Chaturvedi says: “Our results show simple material choices could make a meaningful difference to how satellites affect astronomical observations without major changes to mission design.”

opportunities-81ea46517d.headline: Jaipur Literature Festival Turns Twenty In January 2027
opportunities-81ea46517d.fulltext:
- Since its inception in 2006, the Jaipur Literature Festival has played host to over 8,000 writers, speakers and artists.
- With the continued support of the Government of Rajasthan, the Festival has evolved from a gathering of writers and readers in Jaipur into one of the world’s most recognised literary platforms.
- The 20th edition of the Festival will revolve around the theme ‘20 Years of Ideas. Stories. Conversations’.
As the Jaipur Literature Festival (JLF) gears up to celebrate its 20th edition next year, the Festival marks two remarkable decades of creating spaces where writers, thinkers, artists and audiences come together to engage with books, ideas and conversations that shape our understanding of the world. The 20th edition of the Festival will be held in Jaipur from January 14 to 18, 2027, bringing together leading voices from literature, culture, academia and the arts.
With the continued support of the Government of Rajasthan, the Festival has evolved from a gathering of writers and readers in Jaipur into one of the world’s most recognised literary platforms, transforming the way literature is experienced, discussed and accessed by audiences across India and globally.
Sanjoy K. Roy, Managing Director, Teamwork Arts & Producer, JLF, said in a statement, “What has sustained the Festival is the generosity of our writers, the curiosity of our audiences, and a shared commitment to dialogue across languages, cultures and perspectives… We celebrate that journey while looking ahead to the many conversations still to come."
Since its inception in 2006, the Festival has played host to over 8,000 writers, speakers and artists, welcomed over five million visitors on-ground, and reached an estimated one billion-plus audiences through digital platforms, broadcast partnerships and media networks. It has played a significant role in shaping India’s contemporary literary and cultural ecosystem, creating a shared space where conversations move across literature, history, politics, science, philosophy, arts and contemporary culture.
With more than 15 editions across countries today, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Spain, Australia, the Middle East, the Maldives and Ireland, the Festival has grown into a bridge that connects India's literary traditions with international audiences while bringing global conversations into dialogue with Indian perspectives.
Over the years, the Jaipur Literature Festival has hosted some of the most influential voices across literature, culture and public life, including Nobel Laureates, Booker Prize winners, heads of state, economists, philosophers, artists and global thinkers.
The Festival’s journey has also been marked by a sustained commitment to multilingual storytelling and cultural plurality. Through multilingual programming, translation initiatives and sessions featuring writers across Indian and international languages it has created pathways for regional voices and literary traditions to reach wider audiences, reflecting its belief that every language carries stories, histories, and perspectives that enrich the wider cultural conversation. “The soul of India lies in her literary heritage and linguistic diversity,” Namita Gokhale, author and co-director of JLF, noted in a statement. “It is only appropriate that we celebrate our milestone 20th year with a tribute to her many languages through our ‘Bhasha Swarmala’ series.”
In a conflict-ridden world, literature acts as the glue that holds humanity together. The Jaipur Literature Festival continues to be a living manifestation of that space where stories, languages and ideas bridge divides, reminding us that dialogue is more urgent than ever.
